title: Care Visit Brief
user: People with a new or fluctuating chronic condition who need to give a clinician an accurate, short history of symptoms, triggers, and what changed between appointments.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The asker says they quit six illness-tracking systems—apps, paper, Sheets, and notes—after 2–4 weeks and asks what actually works; the thread has 34 top-level replies.
The issue frames the job directly: students cannot reconstruct when symptoms started, changed, or improved by the time they see a doctor.

recurrence: Two 2026 requests identify the same failure mode: detailed journals are abandoned, leaving an appointment-critical history unrecoverable. The HN request drew 34 replies.
current_workaround: Try a notes app, paper journal, spreadsheet, or a broad health tracker; reconstruct the story from memory at the visit.
incumbents_and_gap: Bearable, Guava, Apple Health, and generic journals collect lots of fields. The gap is an ultra-low-friction local log that turns sparse entries into a clinician-readable chronology without diagnosis or a cloud account.
smallest_useful_product: Offline PWA with one-tap symptom severity, optional trigger/medication tags, a missed-day-safe timeline, and a printable one-page visit brief. Non-goals: diagnosis, care advice, insurance billing, wearables, or clinician portals.
success_measure: In a four-week pilot, 60% of users record on 20+ days and export a visit brief before an appointment.
monetization: one-time — a sensitive personal log must remain useful without a subscription or data sale.
constraints: Health data stays on device by default; clear medical disclaimer; encrypted export option; never infer conditions or make treatment recommendations.
why_distinct: The output is a truthful appointment handoff built from intentionally tiny inputs, not another comprehensive symptom database.

title: Dose Count Compass
user: People managing inhalers, sprays, injectables, or other non-pill medicines who need to know remaining doses and refill risk without making a full medication-management account.

evidence.quote_or_summary: An adult asks how to do a practical personal health audit, showing demand for actionable day-to-day health organization rather than another content feed.
A medTimer user explains that pill-style countdowns do not fit inhalers and sprays, which have physical units plus puffs/sprays, and requests type-specific counts.

recurrence: A 2025 feature request names a concrete medication-format gap; 2026 health-audit discussion shows the broader self-management context. Running out of a rescue or maintenance medicine is high-severity.
current_workaround: Mentally estimate remaining doses, keep a paper tally, use a generic pill reminder, or buy duplicates early.
incumbents_and_gap: Medisafe, MyTherapy, and medTimer focus on reminders and pill inventory. They do not make device-specific remaining-dose confidence, spare-device rotation, and refill lead time the small core workflow.
smallest_useful_product: Offline mobile PWA for a small list of medicines with pill/puff/spray/device counters, quick dose logging, refill threshold, and a printable inventory card. Non-goals: prescription ordering, pharmacy integration, medical advice, or adherence scoring.
success_measure: At least 70% of pilot users still log a dose after 30 days, and no pilot reports an unanticipated empty tracked device.
monetization: one-time — dependable offline tracking is a safety utility, not a recurring content service.
constraints: On-device data only by default; notification permissions must be optional; do not imply stock figures replace device indicators or pharmacist advice.
why_distinct: It handles the physical counting model of medicines people actually use, rather than bolting another reminder onto a pill-centric tracker.

title: Nutrient Floor
user: Home cooks who want to plan a few meals that reliably clear personally chosen fibre, protein, or sugar limits without obsessively logging every calorie.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A successful calorie-tracking user reports Yazio slowness and a broken recipe-sharing workflow, despite losing about 30 lb with it.
Users request planning and tracking of fibre, sugars, and saturated fat alongside macronutrients (10 reactions).

recurrence: Two 2025 requests expose friction in calorie-centric products and the recurring need to plan specific nutritional floors/limits rather than only macros.
current_workaround: Log meals in Yazio/Cronometer, inspect labels manually, or maintain nutrient targets in a spreadsheet.
incumbents_and_gap: Yazio, MyFitnessPal, and Cronometer are broad food diaries. The unresolved gap is a private, meal-first planner that answers 'will this small menu meet my chosen floor?' without a diary, ads, or a food social network.
smallest_useful_product: Local PWA with a saved-food list, 3–5 custom nutrient targets, simple recipe portions, and a weekly coverage view. Non-goals: weight-loss coaching, barcode catalog hosting, medical nutrition therapy, or AI meal generation.
success_measure: 50% of pilot users plan at least three meals per week and can identify one recurring nutrient shortfall in the first month.
monetization: one-time — users should own sensitive food habits and manually entered nutrition data.
constraints: Nutrition values must be visibly user-supplied or sourced with attribution; no medical claims; avoid collecting eating-disorder-sensitive data by default.
why_distinct: It plans minimum nutrition coverage from a small trusted pantry instead of competing as a calorie-counting social database.

title: Batch Cart
user: People cooking several recipes for a household or event who need a single accurate shopping list after changing servings for each recipe.

evidence.quote_or_summary: An HN maker describes a personal micro-app that turns a set of recipes into one consolidated, metric shopping list for two people.
A Cookbook user requests selecting multiple recipes, adjusting each portion count, automatically combining quantities, and exporting the result for family dinners and events.

recurrence: Two independent July 2025 requests describe the exact multi-recipe aggregation job. Errors cause duplicate purchases and last-minute missing ingredients.
current_workaround: Copy ingredients by hand to a notes app, use a spreadsheet, or wire recipes through an LLM and task app.
incumbents_and_gap: Paprika, Mealie, CookBook, and AnyList support recipes and lists, but aggregation varies by host/app and commonly leaves units, pantry exclusions, and package choices to manual cleanup.
smallest_useful_product: Browser-local recipe cards or pasted ingredients; per-recipe servings; deterministic unit-aware aggregation; pantry checkbox exclusions; and a print/share shopping list. Non-goals: recipe scraping, grocery delivery, nutrition advice, or social recipes.
success_measure: A pilot household creates four multi-recipe carts and reports fewer than one duplicate/missing ingredient incident per cart.
monetization: one-time — it is a compact household calculator with no need for marketplace commissions.
constraints: Use only user-entered/imported recipes; preserve original units and show uncertain conversions; no retailer or copyrighted recipe corpus required.
why_distinct: The central artifact is a deterministic, editable multi-recipe purchase calculation—not a recipe site or a thin LLM shopping-list wrapper.

title: Recipe Passport
user: People leaving a recipe app or tired of ad-heavy recipe pages who need to preserve their own recipes in a portable, calm offline cooking format.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The maker says recipe sites are broken and offers a tool that reduces a pasted recipe URL to ingredients and steps, without life story or ads.
A KitchenOwl user asks for Paprika 3 JSON import so they do not have to manually transfer their existing recipes (6 reactions).

recurrence: 2025 portability demand and a 2026 reaction to recipe-page clutter point to ownership and calm consumption, not recipe discovery, as the problem.
current_workaround: Keep Paprika locked to one ecosystem, copy pages into notes, print recipes, or use an ad-blocker and browser reader mode.
incumbents_and_gap: Paprika, Recipe Keeper, Mealie, and KitchenOwl all store recipes. The gap is a no-account local migration and export utility that normalizes personal exports into durable recipe cards without becoming a hosted collection service.
smallest_useful_product: Static-web importer for Paprika JSON and manually pasted structured recipes, producing a local searchable cookbook plus clean print/PDF/JSON export. Non-goals: scraping paywalled sites, publishing a recipe directory, meal delivery, or AI rewriting.
success_measure: At least 80% of test imports retain title, ingredients, steps, yield, and notes; 50% of users export their cookbook after import.
monetization: free — portability is the trust-building wedge; a paid desktop importer could follow only if format maintenance warrants it.
constraints: Import only user-provided files or content; retain recipe provenance; avoid scraping/copyright-dependent distribution; all processing in-browser.
why_distinct: It is a data-portability and offline-reading tool rather than another recipe manager trying to own the user's collection.

title: Garden Care Map
user: Small-space gardeners who need to remember what is planted where, what care happened there, and how irrigation physically reaches each bed.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A plant-app builder includes plant health reports and care reminders among the core expected features, reflecting demand for ongoing plant-care tracking.
GardenBedPlanner needs irrigation parts placed at real bed-space coordinates rather than a detached schematic, explicitly blocking the integrated garden canvas.

recurrence: The 2025 plant-care feature set and 2026 garden-layout issue converge on a persistent care record tied to physical location. Spatial ambiguity makes irrigation and seasonal handoffs error-prone.
current_workaround: Use a generic plant reminder app plus a hand-drawn bed sketch, photos, and a separate irrigation diagram.
incumbents_and_gap: Planta and Greg emphasize individual houseplant reminders; Gardenize and bed planners emphasize layouts. Few small tools connect a simple physical bed map to care history and irrigation runs while remaining offline.
smallest_useful_product: Offline canvas for beds/containers, plant labels, dated care notes, and simple irrigation line segments with length totals. Non-goals: plant identification, disease diagnosis, weather prediction, seed marketplace, or social sharing.
success_measure: 70% of pilot gardeners consult/update the same map at least weekly for one growing month and can locate every active planting without a separate note.
monetization: one-time — seasonal planning data is personal and useful without a hosted service.
constraints: No agronomic or pesticide advice; optional local-only photos; metric/imperial units; accessibility for color-blind bed labels.
why_distinct: It joins care history to the actual garden geometry, not an AI plant identifier or a decorative garden-design app.

title: Shop Fit Sheet
user: Home makers fitting a cabinet, bench, or storage build into a garage, utility room, or vehicle who need a constraint-first cut/material brief before buying stock.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The asker is specifically exploring practical robots in a garage or home utility room for hardware sorting and other maker/home tasks, demonstrating active planning of constrained workspaces.
A user trying to fit a 1350×800×50 cabinet below a van bed needs two doors and a centre support; the configurator's size warning and missing support block their plan.

recurrence: Two 2026 maker/home-planning threads involve real constrained utility spaces. Fit mistakes waste material and can force a build redesign after purchase.
current_workaround: Measure on paper, use a full CAD package, make a generic cut list, and mentally track clearances and hardware constraints.
incumbents_and_gap: SketchUp, Fusion 360, and CutList Optimizer are powerful but can be excessive for a one-off fitted build. The gap is a lightweight constraint sheet that exposes clearance/support conflicts before optimization.
smallest_useful_product: Offline web calculator for outer envelope, openings, panel thickness, supports, clearances, and stock list; export one printable build sheet. Non-goals: 3D CAD, CNC/G-code, structural engineering certification, or a materials marketplace.
success_measure: In testing, 75% of users identify at least one conflicting dimension or missing clearance before purchasing materials.
monetization: one-time — a focused project calculator should work indefinitely offline.
constraints: Prominent 'verify dimensions/load safety' warning; do not represent output as engineering advice; local files only.
why_distinct: It is a pre-build constraint checker for physically fitted home projects, not a general CAD clone or a bin-packing-only cut-list generator.

title: Home Service Passbook
user: Households that want to remember recurring home care and retain proof of what was done, without tying maintenance to appliance-cloud apps.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A writer asks why consumers now need apps for washing machines amid growing complaint about app overload in connected appliances.
A home-maintenance user requests separate 'repeat every' and 'repeat after completion' semantics, a practical distinction for real recurring household work (11 reactions).

recurrence: A 2025 maintenance feature request and 2026 appliance-app backlash point to a durable, vendor-neutral household log. Missed filter, safety, and seasonal work has material cost.
current_workaround: Use vendor apps, calendar reminders, a spreadsheet, receipts in email, or a generic to-do list that cannot model completion-relative recurrence.
incumbents_and_gap: Home Assistant, Tody, Centriq, and appliance vendor apps are either automation-heavy, cloud/account-based, or device-bound. The gap is a small offline service passport with correct recurrence semantics and proof attachments.
smallest_useful_product: Offline PWA with assets/areas, repeat-every vs repeat-after schedules, completion notes/photo/receipt reference, and a printable history. Non-goals: IoT control, contractor marketplace, automated diagnosis, or warranty claims.
success_measure: After three months, 60% of pilot homes have completed at least five scheduled tasks and can retrieve the last-completed date for every tracked asset in under one minute.
monetization: one-time — homeowners should retain a useful maintenance record even if a service shuts down.
constraints: Local-first attachment storage with explicit export; no safety certification or repair advice; durable backup/import format required.
why_distinct: It treats maintenance history as household-owned paperwork, separate from surveillance-prone appliance control.

title: Chore Receipt
user: Roommates and families who do not care who does a recurring task, but need a trusted low-friction record that it was done and when it becomes due again.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The maintainer of Super Productivity describes eight years of a local-first, no-account task manager and explains the desire not to have work habits tracked.
A Donetick household user requests multiple eligible assignees because they only care that a shared chore gets completed, not which person completes it (10 reactions).

recurrence: The specific 2025 household request and 2026 local-first preference identify a shared-task problem that conventional individual to-do lists solve poorly.
current_workaround: Assign chores to one person, message a group chat, use a whiteboard, or maintain a cloud task board.
incumbents_and_gap: Tody, Sweepy, OurHome, and Donetick offer chore systems, but many center individual assignment, scores, accounts, or notifications. The gap is an offline completion receipt with a shared 'anyone can do it' queue and due-after-completion logic.
smallest_useful_product: Local-network/offline PWA with a household invite QR, unassigned shared chores, one-tap completion receipt, repeat-after option, and neutral history. Non-goals: gamified points, surveillance, parental controls, payroll, or chat.
success_measure: A pilot household logs 80% of tracked recurring chores for four consecutive weeks without a separate group-chat reminder.
monetization: free — frictionless household adoption matters more than extracting a subscription from chore coordination.
constraints: Avoid exposing names/history beyond the household device sync; local QR sync must be opt-in and conflict-safe; no child-data collection.
why_distinct: It minimizes blame and account overhead by recording the outcome, not turning chores into a gamified productivity platform.

title: Placeboard Inventory
user: Households with a kitchen, garage, shed, or multiple homes who need to find a shared item by its physical place and record transfers without a warehouse system.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A user planning a kitchen-mounted home dashboard wants a simple local view of recipes, calendar, and notes—not a complicated smart-home stack.
A Binner user requests one part number in multiple locations, rather than creating duplicate identifiers, because the current single-location model fails physical inventory.

recurrence: Two January 2025 threads point to simple local home interfaces and the inability of single-location inventory models to match reality.
current_workaround: Label bins, make duplicate spreadsheet rows, photograph shelves, or use a garage-oriented inventory tool with separate records per location.
incumbents_and_gap: HomeBox, Grocy, Sortly, and Binner manage inventory, but many are asset/catalog-centric or treat a location as a single field. The gap is a household placeboard where one item can live in several places and transfers are first-class.
smallest_useful_product: Offline PWA with a visual place tree (home/room/shelf/bin), multi-location quantities, move history, quick text search, and print labels. Non-goals: barcode-product database, insurance valuation, multi-tenant warehouse workflows, or cloud photos.
success_measure: At least 75% of pilot search tasks locate a tracked item in under 30 seconds, and users record 20+ moves in the first month.
monetization: one-time — local storage inventory should not require an ongoing cloud plan.
constraints: Private on-device inventory; export/import JSON/CSV; avoid implying it is an insurance inventory; accessible text labels must not rely only on color.
why_distinct: Its model is 'where can I find this?' across real household places, rather than a generic asset catalog or pantry scanner.

title: Bills Runway
user: People who know their regular obligations but need a trustworthy near-term cash runway without bank connections or a full envelope-budget overhaul.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The asker tried Plaid-based budgeting tools without success and explicitly wants daily/weekly visibility of spending; the thread has 42 top-level replies.
An Actual Budget user requests schedule-based forecasting and running-balance reports; the issue has 48 reactions.

recurrence: Two January 2025 requests identify a gap between transaction dashboards and a plain answer to 'what will my balance be after the obligations I already know about?'; both attracted substantial engagement.
current_workaround: Use a spreadsheet, calendar plus bank balance, a Plaid dashboard, or a full zero-based budget that users often abandon.
incumbents_and_gap: YNAB, Monarch, Actual Budget, and Copilot are capable budgeting suites. The gap is a small manual, privacy-first runway calculator that deliberately limits scope to balance, dated obligations, and cash buffer.
smallest_useful_product: Offline PWA with starting balance, recurring/one-off bills, paydays, optional manual spending, and a 30/60-day daily balance projection with a low-buffer alert. Non-goals: bank sync, investment tracking, credit scoring, payment initiation, or tax advice.
success_measure: In a 30-day pilot, 70% of users update the runway weekly and can name their next projected low-balance date without opening their bank app.
monetization: one-time — avoiding Plaid and hosted financial-data costs makes a durable paid utility credible.
constraints: No financial advice or execution; all financial inputs local by default; clear manual-entry and date/timezone behavior; encrypted backup optional.
why_distinct: It is a narrow cash-calendar answer, not another expense categorizer, transaction aggregator, or autonomous money tool.

title: Spend Pulse
user: People who repeatedly abandon bloated finance apps but still want a small, private daily or weekly prompt showing whether discretionary spending is on pace.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The asker says they quit popular personal-finance apps because of paywalls, bloated/up-sell UX, $100+ annual pricing, and fragmented tools, and asks others why they stopped.
A new Actual Budget user says schedules represent expenses they must remember and specifically requests notifications for them.

recurrence: The 2026 HN thread identifies retention failures in finance software; a separate 2026 budgeting request calls for timely schedule reminders. The pain is repeated, not a one-time import problem.
current_workaround: Ignore the budget until month-end, use a generic reminder, check a bank app, or maintain a manual spreadsheet.
incumbents_and_gap: Actual Budget, YNAB, Monarch, and PocketGuard provide broad budget systems. The gap is a deliberately tiny manual spend cadence: one category set, one pace target, one respectful offline notification.
smallest_useful_product: Offline PWA with a weekly discretionary allowance, a one-tap amount entry, a rolling pace indicator, and optional on-device daily/weekly notification. Non-goals: transaction import, account aggregation, investment views, credit products, or AI coaching.
success_measure: At least 50% of pilots record spending on 20 of 30 days and open fewer than one finance app besides their bank during that period.
monetization: free — no account, data brokerage, or bank sync makes a lightweight free utility viable and trustworthy.
constraints: No cloud data by default; notification permission is explicit and never nagging; no financial advice or claims that the app improves credit/wealth.
why_distinct: It replaces account-heavy finance dashboards with a single habit loop for spending pace, not a thin chat-based money coach.
